[[File:Plane equation qtl3.svg|thumb|Plane equation in normal form]]

In [[Euclidean geometry]], a '''plane''' is a [[Flat space|flat]] two-[[dimension]]al [[surface (geometry)|surface]] that extends indefinitely. 
[[Euclidean plane]]s often arise as [[Euclidean subspace|subspaces]] of [[three-dimensional space]] <math>\mathbb{R}^3</math>.
A prototypical example is one of a room's walls, infinitely extended and assumed infinitesimally thin.
While a pair of real numbers <math>\mathbb{R}^2</math> suffices to describe points on a plane, the relationship with out-of-plane points requires special consideration for their [[embedding]] in the [[ambient space]] <math>\mathbb{R}^3</math>.

==Derived concepts==
A '''{{vanchor|plane segment}}''' or '''{{vanchor|planar region}}''' (or simply "plane", in lay use) is a planar surface [[region (mathematics)|region]]; it is analogous to a [[line segment]].
A ''[[bivector]]'' is an [[Orientation (geometry)|oriented]] plane segment, analogous to [[directed line segment]]s.{{efn|More precisely, an algebraic entity analogous to an [[equivalence class]] of oriented plane segments.}}
A ''[[face (geometry)|face]]'' is a plane segment bounding a [[solid object]].<ref>{{cite book | title = [[Merriam-Webster's Collegiate Dictionary]] | edition = Eleventh | publisher = [[Merriam-Webster]] | location = Springfield, MA | year = 2004}}</ref>
A ''[[slab (geometry)|slab]]'' is a region bounded by two parallel planes.
A ''[[parallelepiped]]'' is a region bounded by three pairs of parallel planes.

==Background==
{{Main|Euclidean geometry}}

[[Euclid]] set forth the first great landmark of mathematical thought, an axiomatic treatment of geometry.<ref>{{harvnb|Eves|1963|loc=p. 19}}</ref> He selected a small core of undefined terms (called ''common notions'') and postulates (or [[axiom]]s) which he then used to prove various geometrical statements. Although the plane in its modern sense is not directly given a definition anywhere in the ''[[Euclid's Elements|Elements]]'', it may be thought of as part of the common notions.<ref>{{Citation
|last= Joyce
|first= D. E.|author-link=David E. Joyce (mathematician)
|title= Euclid's Elements, Book I, Definition 7
|publisher= Clark University
|year= 1996
|url= http://aleph0.clarku.edu/~djoyce/java/elements/bookI/defI7.html 
|access-date= 8 August 2009}}</ref> Euclid never used numbers to measure length, angle, or area. The Euclidean plane equipped with a chosen [[Cartesian coordinate system]] is called a ''Cartesian plane''; a non-Cartesian Euclidean plane equipped with a [[polar coordinate system]] would be called a ''polar plane''.
<!--In higher-dimensional Euclidean space, a plane inside this space can be uniquely determined by any of the following sets of objects:
* three [[non-collinear points]] (i.e. not lying on the same [[line (mathematics)|line]])
* a line and a point not on the line
* two distinct intersecting lines -->
[[File:Planes parallel.svg|thumb|right|150px|Three parallel planes]]
<!--In 3 dimensional Euclidean space, planes, like [[line (geometry)|lines]], can be [[parallel (geometry)|parallel]] or intersecting. Lines drawn on two parallel planes will either be parallel or [[skew lines|skew]] but will not intersect. Intersecting planes may be [[perpendicular]] or may form any number of other angles. In Euclidean spaces of more than 3 dimensions, it is possible to have two planes that intersect in a single point.-->

A plane is a [[ruled surface]].

===Euclidean plane===
{{excerpt|Euclidean plane|templates=-General geometry}}

==Representation==
This section is solely concerned with planes embedded in three dimensions: specifically, in [[Cartesian product|{{math|'''R'''<sup>3</sup>}}]].

===Determination by contained points and lines===
In a Euclidean space of any number of dimensions, a plane is uniquely determined by any of the following:
* Three non-[[collinear]] points (points not on a single line).
* A line and a point not on that line.
* Two distinct but intersecting lines.
* Two distinct but [[parallel (geometry)|parallel]] lines.

===Properties===
The following statements hold in three-dimensional Euclidean space but not in higher dimensions, though they have higher-dimensional analogues:
* Two distinct planes are either parallel or they intersect in a [[line (geometry)|line]].
* A line is either parallel to a plane, intersects it at a single point, or is contained in the plane.
* Two distinct lines [[perpendicular]] to the same plane must be parallel to each other.
* Two distinct planes perpendicular to the same line must be parallel to each other.

===Point–normal form and general form of the equation of a plane{{anchor|Point–normal form}}===
In a manner analogous to the way lines in a two-dimensional space are described using a point-slope form for their equations, planes in a three dimensional space have a natural description using a point in the plane and a vector orthogonal to it (the [[normal vector]]) to indicate its "inclination".

Specifically, let {{math|'''''r'''''<sub>0</sub>}} be the position vector of some point {{math|1=''P''<sub>0</sub> = (''x''<sub>0</sub>, ''y''<sub>0</sub>, ''z''<sub>0</sub>)}}, and let {{math|1='''''n''''' = (''a'', ''b'', ''c'')}} be a nonzero vector. The plane determined by the point {{math|''P''<sub>0</sub>}} and the vector {{mvar|'''n'''}} consists of those points {{math|''P''}}, with position vector {{mvar|'''r'''}}, such that the vector drawn from {{math|''P''<sub>0</sub>}} to {{math|''P''}} is perpendicular to {{mvar|'''n'''}}. Recalling that two vectors are perpendicular if and only if their dot product is zero, it follows that the desired plane can be described as the set of all points {{mvar|'''r'''}} such that
<math display="block">\boldsymbol{n} \cdot (\boldsymbol{r}-\boldsymbol{r}_0)=0.</math>
The dot here means a [[dot product|dot (scalar) product]].<br>
Expanded this becomes
<math display="block"> a (x-x_0) + b(y-y_0) + c(z-z_0) = 0,</math>
which is the ''point–normal'' form of the equation of a plane.<ref>{{harvnb|Anton|1994|loc=p. 155}}</ref> This is just a [[linear equation]]
<math display="block"> ax + by + cz + d = 0,</math>
where
<math display="block"> d = -(ax_0 + by_0 + cz_0),</math>
which is the expanded form of <math>- \boldsymbol{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{r}_0.</math>

In mathematics it is a common convention to express the normal as a [[unit vector]], but the above argument holds for a normal vector of any non-zero length.

Conversely, it is easily shown that if {{math|''a''}}, {{math|''b''}}, {{math|''c''}}, and {{math|''d''}} are constants and {{math|''a''}}, {{math|''b''}}, and {{math|''c''}} are not all zero, then the graph of the equation
<math display="block"> ax + by + cz + d = 0,</math>
is a plane having the vector {{math|1='''''n''''' = (''a'', ''b'', ''c'')}} as a normal.<ref>{{harvnb|Anton|1994|loc=p. 156}}</ref> This familiar equation for a plane is called the ''general form'' of the equation of the plane or just the ''plane equation''.<ref name=Weisstein2009>{{Citation
|title= Plane
|url= http://mathworld.wolfram.com/Plane.html
|year= 2009
|author= Weisstein, Eric W.
|journal= MathWorld--A Wolfram Web Resource
|access-date= 2009-08-08
}}</ref>

Thus for example a [[regression equation]] of the form {{math|1=''y'' = ''d'' + ''ax'' + ''cz''}} (with {{math|1=''b'' = −1}}) establishes a best-fit plane in three-dimensional space when there are two explanatory variables.

===Describing a plane with a point and two vectors lying on it===
Alternatively, a plane may be described parametrically as the set of all points of the form
<math display="block">\boldsymbol{r} = \boldsymbol{r}_0 + s \boldsymbol{v} + t \boldsymbol{w},</math>

[[File:PlaneR.jpg|thumb|Vector description of a plane]]
where {{mvar|s}} and {{mvar|t}} range over all real numbers, {{mvar|'''v'''}} and {{mvar|'''w'''}} are given [[linear independence|linearly independent]] [[vector (geometry)|vectors]] defining the plane, and {{math|'''''r'''''<sub>0</sub>}} is the vector representing the position of an arbitrary (but fixed) point on the plane. The vectors {{mvar|'''v'''}} and {{mvar|'''w'''}} can be visualized as vectors starting at {{math|'''''r'''''<sub>0</sub>}} and pointing in different [[Direction (geometry)|directions]] along the plane. The vectors {{mvar|'''v'''}} and {{mvar|'''w'''}} can be [[perpendicular]], but cannot be parallel.

===Describing a plane through three points===
Let {{math|1='''''p'''''<sub>1</sub> = (''x''<sub>1</sub>, ''y''<sub>1</sub>, ''z''<sub>1</sub>)}}, {{math|1='''''p'''''<sub>2</sub> = (''x''<sub>2</sub>, ''y''<sub>2</sub>, ''z''<sub>2</sub>)}}, and {{math|1='''''p'''''<sub>3</sub> = (''x''<sub>3</sub>, ''y''<sub>3</sub>, ''z''<sub>3</sub>)}} be non-collinear points.

====Method 1====
The plane passing through {{math|'''''p'''''<sub>1</sub>}}, {{math|'''''p'''''<sub>2</sub>}}, and {{math|'''''p'''''<sub>3</sub>}} can be described as the set of all points (''x'',''y'',''z'') that satisfy the following [[determinant]] equations:
<math display="block">\begin{vmatrix}
x - x_1 & y - y_1 & z - z_1 \\
x_2 - x_1 & y_2 - y_1 & z_2 - z_1 \\
x_3 - x_1 & y_3 - y_1 & z_3 - z_1
\end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix}
x - x_1 & y - y_1 & z - z_1 \\
x - x_2 & y - y_2 & z - z_2 \\
x - x_3 & y - y_3 & z - z_3
\end{vmatrix} = 0. </math>

====Method 2====
To describe the plane by an equation of the form <math> ax + by + cz + d = 0 </math>, solve the following system of equations:
<math display="block"> ax_1 + by_1 + cz_1 + d = 0</math>
<math display="block"> ax_2 + by_2 + cz_2 + d = 0</math>
<math display="block"> ax_3 + by_3 + cz_3 + d = 0.</math>

This system can be solved using [[Cramer's rule]] and basic matrix manipulations. Let
<math display="block">D = \begin{vmatrix}
x_1 & y_1 & z_1 \\
x_2 & y_2 & z_2 \\
x_3 & y_3 & z_3
\end{vmatrix}.</math>

If {{math|''D''}} is non-zero (so for planes not through the origin) the values for {{math|''a''}}, {{math|''b''}} and {{math|''c''}} can be calculated as follows:
<math display="block">a = \frac{-d}{D} \begin{vmatrix}
1 & y_1 & z_1 \\
1 & y_2 & z_2 \\
1 & y_3 & z_3
\end{vmatrix}</math>
<math display="block">b = \frac{-d}{D} \begin{vmatrix}
x_1 & 1 & z_1 \\
x_2 & 1 & z_2 \\
x_3 & 1 & z_3
\end{vmatrix}</math>
<math display="block">c = \frac{-d}{D} \begin{vmatrix}
x_1 & y_1 & 1 \\
x_2 & y_2 & 1 \\
x_3 & y_3 & 1
\end{vmatrix}.</math>

These equations are parametric in ''d''. Setting ''d'' equal to any non-zero number and substituting it into these equations will yield one solution set.

====Method 3====
This plane can also be described by the {{Section link|Euclidean planes in three-dimensional space|Point–normal form and general form of the equation of a plane|nopage=y}} prescription above. A suitable normal vector is given by the [[cross product]]
<math display="block">\boldsymbol n = ( \boldsymbol p_2 - \boldsymbol p_1 ) \times ( \boldsymbol p_3 - \boldsymbol p_1 ), </math>
and the point {{math|'''''r'''''<sub>0</sub>}} can be taken to be any of the given points {{math|'''''p'''''<sub>1</sub>}}, {{math|'''''p'''''<sub>2</sub>}} or {{math|'''''p'''''<sub>3</sub>}}<ref name=PaulsPlanes>{{citation
|last= Dawkins
|first= Paul
|title= Calculus III
|chapter= Equations of Planes
|chapter-url= http://tutorial.math.lamar.edu/Classes/CalcIII/EqnsOfPlanes.aspx
}}</ref> (or any other point in the plane).

==Occurrence in nature==
{{see also|Surface#In the physical sciences}}
[[File:Plane wave wavefronts 3D.svg|thumb|left|The [[wavefront]]s of a plane wave traveling in [[3-space]]]]

A plane serves as a mathematical model for many physical phenomena, such as [[specular reflection]] in a [[plane mirror]] or [[wavefront]]s in a [[traveling plane wave]].
The [[free surface]] of undisturbed liquids tends to be nearly flat (see [[flatness (liquids)|flatness]]).
The flattest surface ever manufactured is a quantum-stabilized atom mirror.<ref name="Evans 2008">{{cite web | last=Evans | first=Jon | title=Smoothest surface ever is a mirror for atoms | website=New Scientist | date=2008-08-22 | url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn14587-smoothest-surface-ever-is-a-mirror-for-atoms/ | access-date=2023-03-05}}</ref>
In astronomy, various ''[[reference plane]]s'' are used to define positions in orbit.
''[[Anatomical plane]]s'' may be lateral ("sagittal"), frontal ("coronal") or transversal.
In geology, ''[[bed (geology)|beds]]'' (layers of sediments) often are planar.
Planes are involved in different forms of [[imaging]], such as the ''[[focal plane]]'', ''[[picture plane]]'', and ''[[image plane]]''. 
[[File:Webysther 20211009102044 - Parque Geológico do Varvito.jpg|thumb|Beds of sedimentary rock at Parque Geológico do Varvito, [[Itu, São Paulo]], Brazil]]

=== Miller indices ===
{{Main|Miller index}}
[[File:Miller Indices Cubes2.svg|thumb|150px|Planes with different Miller indices in cubic crystals]]
The attitude of a [[lattice plane]] is the orientation of the line normal to the plane,<ref name=Granville>
{{cite book |author=William Anthony Granville |title=Elements of the Differential and Integral Calculus |page=[https://archive.org/details/elementsdiffere02goog/page/n293 275] |url=https://archive.org/details/elementsdiffere02goog |chapter=§178 Normal line to a surface |publisher=Ginn & Company |year=1904
}}</ref> and is described by the plane's [[Miller indices]]. In three-space a family of planes (a series of parallel planes) can be denoted by its [[Miller indices]] (''hkl''),<ref name=Love>
{{cite book |title=A Treatise on the Mathematical Theory of Elasticity| volume=1 |author=Augustus Edward Hough Love |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-GkSAAAAIAAJ&pg=PA79 |page=79 ''ff'' |year=1892 |publisher=Cambridge University Press
}}</ref><ref name=Ladd>
{{cite book |author1=Marcus Frederick Charles Ladd |author2=Rex Alfred Palmer |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vNJrAe36BBMC&pg=PA62 |chapter=§2.3 Families of planes and interplanar spacings |page=62 ''ff'' |isbn=0-306-47454-9 |edition=4th |publisher=Springer |year=2003 |title=Structure Determination by X-Ray Crystallography
}}</ref> so the family of planes has an attitude common to all its constituent planes.

=== Strike and dip ===
{{Main|Strike and dip}}
[[File:StrikeLine&Dip.JPG|thumb|150px|left|Strike line and dip of a plane describing attitude relative to a horizontal plane and a vertical plane perpendicular to the strike line]]
Many features observed in geology are planes or lines, and their orientation is commonly referred to as their ''attitude''. These attitudes are specified with two angles.

For a line, these angles are called the ''trend'' and the ''plunge''. The trend is the compass direction of the line, and the plunge is the downward angle it makes with a horizontal plane.<ref name=Rowland>
{{cite book |title=Structural Analysis and Synthesis: A Laboratory Course in Structural Geology |author1=Stephen Mark Rowland |author2=Ernest M. Duebendorfer |author3=Ilsa M. Schiefelbein |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IWnmBEtmg2MC&q=%22attitude+of+a+line%22&pg=PR3 |chapter=Attitudes of lines and planes |isbn=978-1-4051-1652-7 |edition=3rd |publisher=Wiley-Blackwell |year=2007 |page=1 ''ff''
}}</ref>

For a plane, the two angles are called its ''strike (angle)'' and its ''dip (angle)''. A ''strike line'' is the intersection of a horizontal plane with the observed planar feature (and therefore a horizontal line), and the strike angle is the ''bearing'' of this line (that is, relative to [[True north|geographic north]] or from [[Magnetic declination|magnetic north]]). The dip is the angle between a horizontal plane and the observed planar feature as observed in a third vertical plane perpendicular to the strike line.
